The Weight Gram Matrix Captures
Sequential Feature Linearization in Deep Networks

Taehun Cha Affiliation: Department of Mathematics Affiliation: Korea University Email: cth127@korea.ac.kr    Daniel Beaglehole Affiliation: Computer Science and Engineering Affiliation: UC San Diego Email: dbeaglehole@ucsd.edu    Adityanarayanan Radhakrishnan Affiliation: MIT Mathematics Affiliation: Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard Email: aradha@mit.edu    Donghun Lee Thanks: Corresponding author. Affiliation: Department of Mathematics Affiliation: Korea University Email: holy@korea.ac.kr
Abstract

Understanding how deep neural networks learn representations remains a central challenge in machine learning theory. In this work, we propose a feature-centric framework for analyzing neural network training by relating weight updates to feature evolution. We introduce a simple identity, the Feature Learning Equation, which identifies the weight Gram matrix as the key object capturing feature dynamics. This enables us to interpret gradient descent as implicitly inducing a hypothetical evolution of features, whose covariance structure — termed the Virtual Covariance — characterizes how representations evolve during training. Building on this perspective, we introduce Target Linearity, a measure quantifying the linear alignment between features and targets. By analyzing the training and layer-wise dynamics, we show that deep networks learn to sequentially transform representations toward target-linear structure. This linearization perspective provides a unified interpretation of several empirical phenomena, including Neural Collapse and linear interpolation in generative models. Code is available at https://github.com/cth127/GramLin.

1 Introduction

Feature learning is central to the success of deep neural networks, yet a unified account of how representations evolve during training remains limited. Existing work falls into two directions. General theories of training dynamics are largely parameter-centric, as in kernel-based analyses where features remain effectively fixed [16]. In contrast, recent work studies feature learning through analytically tractable case studies — e.g., single and multi-index models, staircase, polynomials, and teacher-student setups — showing that networks can provably learn task-relevant representations [1, 3, 10, 11]. However, these results rely on specific problem structures, leaving open how feature learning behaves in general, realistic, high-dimensional settings.

A natural way to address this gap is to analyze training directly in feature space. As a thought experiment, suppose that instead of updating weights, we directly update hidden features by following the loss gradient. Concretely, fix the input xx and define a virtual trajectory x~t\tilde{x}_{t} that accumulates the feature-space gradient at each training step:

x~t+1←x~t−γ​∇xℒt,x~0=x,\tilde{x}_{t+1}\leftarrow\tilde{x}_{t}-\gamma\nabla_{x}\mathcal{L}_{t},\qquad\tilde{x}_{0}=x,

where ∇xℒt\nabla_{x}\mathcal{L}_{t} is computed under the network with parameters θt\theta_{t} with usual gradient descent update (GD) at step tt. We call x~t\tilde{x}_{t} the virtual update of xx. Note that x~t\tilde{x}_{t} does not affect the actual training trajectory; it tracks, in feature space, the direction GD would move features if features were the optimization variables. Figure 1 shows that the virtual update progressively unrolls Swiss roll data into a linear form. This raises a natural question: although GD operates in weight space, does it implicitly induce this feature-space evolution? Answering it requires a tool that connects weight-space updates to feature-space dynamics.

Such a tool follows directly from the chain rule. We begin by introducing a simple identity relating gradients in weight space to gradients in input (or hidden) space. For any function of the form f⁡(z)f(z) with z=W​hz=Wh, the chain rule yields

∇hf=W⊤​∇zfand∇Wf=∇zf⋅h⊤\nabla_{h}f=W^{\top}\nabla_{z}f\quad\text{and}\quad\nabla_{W}f=\nabla_{z}f\cdot h^{\top}

Combining these gives

∇hf⋅h⊤=W⊤​∇Wf.\nabla_{h}f\cdot h^{\top}=W^{\top}\nabla_{W}f. (1)

The left-hand side describes how features evolve; the right-hand side describes how weights update. The equation allows us to translate between the two, and in particular, it identifies the weight Gram matrix W⊤​WW^{\top}W as the natural object connecting them. We refer to this exact identity as the Feature Learning Equation, and use it throughout the paper to analyze feature evolution.

In Section 2, we examine the role of the weight Gram matrix more closely and present empirical evidence that it carries the dominant signal of feature learning. This enables us to analyze what the weight Gram matrix learns and, in turn, how hidden features evolve during training — i.e., feature learning. Building on this perspective, we make four theoretical contributions:

  • •

    Section 3: We prove that the weight Gram matrix learns the Virtual Covariance, which captures the covariance structure of virtually updated hidden states.

  • •

    Section 4.1: We introduce Target Linearity, a novel quantity measuring the linear relationship between hidden states and target labels, where the Gram structure appears again.

  • •

    Section 4.2: We characterize the training and layer-wise dynamics of Target Linearity. The training dynamics reveal that feature learning is a moving-target problem in which the network chases an evolving linear predictor, in contrast to the Neural Tangent Kernel regime (NTK, [16]) where the linear model is fixed. The layer-wise dynamics show that trained networks sequentially linearize input data with respect to the target, consistent with prior empirical findings on linear probes [2].

  • •

    Section 5: We show this linearization perspective can explain other feature learning phenomena. We show Neural Collapse [36] is an extreme case of target linearization, and that high Target Linearity is a sufficient condition for the linear interpolation property observed in the latent space of generative models [42], demonstrating the generality of our framework.

2 Weight Gram Matrix as a Bridge

We now show how Equation 1 surfaces when analyzing the weight Gram matrix. Computing the Gram matrix of the gradient-descent-updated weight matrix yields

(W−γ​∇Wℒ)⊤​(W−γ​∇Wℒ)\displaystyle(W-\gamma\nabla_{W}\mathcal{L})^{\top}(W-\gamma\nabla_{W}\mathcal{L}) =W⊤​W−γ⁡(W⊤​∇Wℒ+∇Wℒ⊤​W)+O⁡(γ2)\displaystyle=W^{\top}W-\gamma(W^{\top}\nabla_{W}\mathcal{L}+\nabla_{W}\mathcal{L}^{\top}W)+O(\gamma^{2}) (2)
≈W⊤​W−γ⁡(∇hℒ⋅h⊤+h⋅∇hℒ⊤).\displaystyle\approx W^{\top}W-\gamma(\nabla_{h}\mathcal{L}\cdot h^{\top}+h\cdot\nabla_{h}\mathcal{L}^{\top}).

where ℒ\mathcal{L} is the loss function and γ\gamma is the learning rate. This identity makes a key point clear: by taking the Gram of the weight matrix, we can directly access feature-space gradients and, through them, feature evolution.

The weight Gram matrix is not an entirely novel object in the feature learning literature. 39 recently proposed the Neural Feature Ansatz (NFA) as a step toward understanding feature learning in neural networks. They showed that the weight Gram matrix at each layer is closely related to the gradient of the network output with respect to that layer’s input features. For a network ff with ll-th layer weight matrix WlW_{l} and corresponding input representation hlh_{l}, NFA conjectures

Wl⊤​Wl∝𝔼⁡[∇hlf⋅∇hlf⊤],W_{l}^{\top}W_{l}\propto\mathbb{E}\left[\nabla_{h_{l}}f\cdot\nabla_{h_{l}}f^{\top}\right],

where the right-hand side is termed the Average Gradient Outer Product (AGOP). This relationship has been established theoretically in low-rank matrix completion, a widely studied setting for feature learning [40], and has also been validated empirically across a broad range of architectures and datasets.

The discussion so far establishes the weight Gram matrix as a natural object in feature learning analysis, both theoretically (via the FL equation) and through prior empirical observation (via NFA). A sharper question remains: Can the weight Gram matrix sufficiently capture the feature learning dynamics? We test this directly by isolating the Gram-modifying component of the gradient update.

Specifically, we consider an update direction Δ′\Delta^{\prime} that leaves the weight Gram matrix unchanged, found by solving

arg⁡minΔ′⁡‖∇Wℒ−Δ′‖Fsubject toW⊤​Δ′+Δ′⁣⊤​W=0.\arg\min_{\Delta^{\prime}}\|\nabla_{W}\mathcal{L}-\Delta^{\prime}\|_{F}\quad\text{subject to}\quad W^{\top}\Delta^{\prime}+\Delta^{\prime\top}W=0.

Setting Δ=∇Wℒ−Δ′\Delta=\nabla_{W}\mathcal{L}-\Delta^{\prime} and updating W+=W−γ​ΔW^{+}=W-\gamma\Delta yields

(W+)⊤​W+=(W−γ​∇Wℒ)⊤​(W−γ​∇Wℒ)+O⁡(γ2),(W^{+})^{\top}W^{+}=(W-\gamma\nabla_{W}\mathcal{L})^{\top}(W-\gamma\nabla_{W}\mathcal{L})+O(\gamma^{2}),

so the Gram matrix evolves identically to that of standard GD, while the components of the gradient that leave the Gram unchanged are removed. We refer to Δ\Delta as the whitened gradient. If the weight Gram matrix carries the learning signal, training with Δ\Delta should recover the performance of standard GD; if it does not, performance should largely degrade.

We train three-layer fully connected networks on standard image classification benchmarks [22, 25, 34] using both standard GD and the whitened update. Figure 2 reports the results. On MNIST, SVHN, and CIFAR-10, the whitened update matches or exceeds the performance of standard GD; on SVHN and CIFAR-10 specifically, it reaches GD’s best performance within four to five epochs and shows lower variance across runs on SVHN. On CIFAR-100, it tracks standard GD with a small gap. The details for computing Δ\Delta are described in Section B.1. Comparable results for Convolutional architectures [23] are deferred to Section B.2.

These results indicate that the Gram-modifying component of the gradient is largely sufficient to recover standard training performance: the residual component, while present in the gradient, contributes little to feature learning beyond what the Gram update already provides. This empirically substantiates the central role of the weight Gram matrix and motivates the analyses developed in the remainder of the paper, where we ask what the Gram matrix learns (Section 3) and what its evolution achieves at the level of features (Section 4).

3 Weight Gram Learns Virtual Covariance

Section 2 established the weight Gram matrix as a natural and empirically central object in feature learning analysis. We now ask: what does the weight Gram matrix learn during training? We show that each GD step shifts the weight Gram matrix by an amount that captures the covariance structure of virtually updated hidden states — the same virtual update introduced in Section 1. This formalizes the visualization in Figure 1: the Gram matrix tracks how features would evolve if features themselves were the optimization variables.

Settings

We work with a standard LL-layer fully connected network f⁡(x)=w⊤​hLf(x)=w^{\top}h_{L}, where hl∈ℝdlh_{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{l}} denotes the ll-th hidden state, defined recursively as hl=σ⁡(Wl−1​hl−1)h_{l}=\sigma(W_{l-1}h_{l-1}) with h0=x∈ℝd0h_{0}=x\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{0}} and σ\sigma a nonlinear activation function applied element-wise. The vector w∈ℝdLw\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{L}} serves as the final predictor, and Wl∈ℝdl+1×dlW_{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{l+1}\times d_{l}} are the weight matrices. For a loss function ℒ\mathcal{L}, we write ∇Wlℒ∈ℝdl+1×dl\nabla_{W_{l}}\mathcal{L}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{l+1}\times d_{l}} for the gradient with respect to WlW_{l}.

Definition 1.

The virtual update of a hidden state hlh_{l} (or of the input h0=xh_{0}=x) with learning rate γ\gamma is hl+=hl−γ​∇hlℒh^{+}_{l}=h_{l}-\gamma\nabla_{h_{l}}\mathcal{L}. The actual update of a weight matrix WlW_{l} is Wl+=Wl−γ​∇WlℒW^{+}_{l}=W_{l}-\gamma\nabla_{W_{l}}\mathcal{L}, the standard GD step. The Virtual Covariance (VC) is cov~​(hl+)=hl+⋅(hl+)⊤\widetilde{\mathrm{cov}}(h^{+}_{l})=h^{+}_{l}\cdot(h^{+}_{l})^{\top}, and the Virtual Covariance Shift (VCS) is cov~​(hl+)−cov~​(hl)\widetilde{\mathrm{cov}}(h^{+}_{l})-\widetilde{\mathrm{cov}}(h_{l}).

The virtual update represents how the input to the ll-th layer would change under GD if hidden states themselves were the optimization variables. We use the term virtual because GD updates weights, not hidden states directly. The VCS therefore characterizes how the input covariance structure would evolve to reduce the loss.11 1 Strictly, cov~\widetilde{\mathrm{cov}} is not a covariance matrix since hl+h_{l}^{+} and hlh_{l} are not guaranteed to be centered; with standard normalization the two coincide.

Weight Gram Dynamics

The following theorem, our main result for this section, shows that the actual GD update on the weights produces precisely this VCS on the Gram matrix.

Theorem 1.

The shift in the Gram matrix of the gradient-descent-updated weight matrix equals the Virtual Covariance Shift up to O⁡(γ2)O(\gamma^{2}):

(Wl+)⊤​Wl+−Wl⊤​Wl=cov~​(hl+)−cov~​(hl)+O⁡(γ2).(W^{+}_{l})^{\top}W^{+}_{l}-W_{l}^{\top}W_{l}=\widetilde{\mathrm{cov}}(h^{+}_{l})-\widetilde{\mathrm{cov}}(h_{l})+O(\gamma^{2}).

The proof is direct from Equation 2, as cov~​(hl+)−cov~​(hl)=−γ⁡(∇hℒ⋅h⊤+h⋅∇hℒ⊤)+O⁡(γ2)\widetilde{\mathrm{cov}}(h^{+}_{l})-\widetilde{\mathrm{cov}}(h_{l})=-\gamma(\nabla_{h}\mathcal{L}\cdot h^{\top}+h\cdot\nabla_{h}\mathcal{L}^{\top})+O(\gamma^{2}). We show this also holds for Convolutional neural network [23] in Section C.1.

The ii-th column wiw_{i} of WW determines how the ii-th input entry xix_{i} influences the next layer h=σ⁡(W​x)h=\sigma(Wx). The Gram entry (W⊤​W)i​j=wi⊤​wj(W^{\top}W)_{ij}=w_{i}^{\top}w_{j} therefore measures the correlation between the effects of xix_{i} and xjx_{j} on hh. In this sense, the weight Gram matrix is an input covariance with respect to its influence on the next-layer representation, while the VCS describes how this covariance should evolve to reduce the loss. Theorem 1 shows that GD on the weights aligns the two: the actual Gram update tracks the desired covariance shift, even though hidden states are never updated directly. The red dashed contours in Figure 1 make this evolution visible: each contour shows the density of a Gaussian with covariance W⊤​WW^{\top}W at the first layer, adapting with the virtual unrolling of the spiral.

This result clarifies the relationship to the Neural Feature Ansatz of 39, which conjectures W⊤​W∝1N​∑i=1N∇hif⋅∇hif⊤W^{\top}W\propto\tfrac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\nabla_{h_{i}}f\cdot\nabla_{h_{i}}f^{\top} (AGOP). An AGOP-like term — with the network output replaced by the loss — appears within the γ2\gamma^{2} residual of Theorem 1. The VCS therefore refines the AGOP correspondence by capturing the leading-order Gram update directly. Empirically, the VCS tracks the actual Gram update at ρ=0.98\rho=0.98, compared to ρ=0.71\rho=0.71 for AGOP (See Section B.3).

Relationship between Virtual vs. Actual Update

Theorem 1 establishes that the weight Gram matrix learns the covariance structure of virtually updated features. A natural question is whether this is meaningful in practice: does the actually updated hidden state σ⁡(Wl−1+​hl−1)\sigma(W^{+}_{l-1}h_{l-1}) behave similarly to the virtual update hl+h_{l}^{+}? If actual and virtual updates diverge, WlW_{l} may be optimized to expect features that the previous layer never produces. The following proposition, stated for the single-sample case, shows the two are aligned in both sign and magnitude.

Proposition 1.

Assume σ\sigma is LL-Lipschitz and ‖hl−1‖2=1\|h_{l-1}\|_{2}=1, and let Wl−1+W^{+}_{l-1} denote the layer l−1l{-}1 weight matrix after one gradient descent step on the single data point producing hl−1h_{l-1}, with all other layers held fixed. Then |σ⁡(Wl−1+​hl−1)−σ⁡(Wl−1​hl−1)|≤L2​|hl+−hl||\sigma(W^{+}_{l-1}h_{l-1})-\sigma(W_{l-1}h_{l-1})|\leq L^{2}|h_{l}^{+}-h_{l}| element-wise. If σ\sigma is additionally monotonically increasing, then sgn⁡(σ⁡(Wl−1+​hl−1)−σ⁡(Wl−1​hl−1))=sgn⁡(hl+−hl)\mathrm{sgn}(\sigma(W^{+}_{l-1}h_{l-1})-\sigma(W_{l-1}h_{l-1}))=\mathrm{sgn}(h_{l}^{+}-h_{l}); the sign equality also holds for non-decreasing σ\sigma such as ReLU under the convention sgn⁡(0)∈{−1,+1}\mathrm{sgn}(0)\in\{-1,+1\}.

Proposition 1 shows that the actual update on the hidden state agrees with the virtual update in direction and is bounded by it in magnitude. For 1-Lipschitz activations such as ReLU, the magnitude bound reduces to |hl+−hl||h_{l}^{+}-h_{l}| directly. The proof is given in Section C.2.

Together, Theorem 1 and Proposition 1 characterize what the weight Gram matrix learns: it tracks the VC structure that GD would impose on features directly, and the resulting features are realized at the next layer in a controlled way. Figure 1 hints this evolution has a striking geometric consequence — virtually updated features become progressively linear with respect to the target. We turn now to formalizing this observation as Target Linearity.

4 Weight Gram Captures Target Linearity

We now formalize the linearization phenomenon hinted in Section 3. We introduce Target Linearity, a quantitative measure of how well a linear model can predict the target from learned features, and analyze its dynamics during training and across layers. A central technical step is to identify a tractable surrogate that exposes the weight Gram matrix as the object that captures this linearization.

4.1 Target Linearity and its Surrogate

Definition 2.

For a data matrix H=[h1,…,hN]∈ℝdl×NH=[h_{1},\dots,h_{N}]\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{l}\times N} and target vector Y=[y1,…,yN]⊤∈ℝNY=[y_{1},\dots,y_{N}]^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{N}, we define the Target Linearity (TL) as the coefficient of determination (R2R^{2}) of (ridge) linear regression: for λ≥0\lambda\geq 0,

𝒯λ​(H,Y)=1−‖Y−Y^λ‖22‖Y−Y¯‖22,\mathcal{T}_{\lambda}(H,Y)=1-\frac{\|Y-\hat{Y}_{\lambda}\|_{2}^{2}}{\|Y-\bar{Y}\|_{2}^{2}},

where Y^λ=H⊤​(H​H⊤+λ​I)−1​H​Y\hat{Y}_{\lambda}=H^{\top}(HH^{\top}+\lambda I)^{-1}HY, Y¯=y¯⋅𝟏N\bar{Y}=\bar{y}\cdot\mathbf{1}_{N}, and y¯=1N​∑i=1Nyi\bar{y}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}y_{i}.

At λ=0\lambda=0 (and assuming H​H⊤HH^{\top} is invertible), TL recovers the R2R^{2} of ordinary least squares. Since TL is defined as the R2R^{2} score of linear regression, it quantifies how well the target can be explained by a linear function of the features.

The features HH appear in the squared error ‖Y−Y^λ‖22\|Y-\hat{Y}_{\lambda}\|_{2}^{2} through multiple occurrences, making the dependence difficult to analyze directly. Applying the Woodbury identity yields ‖Y−Y^λ‖22=λ2​Y⊤​(λ​I+H⊤​H)−2​Y\|Y-\hat{Y}_{\lambda}\|_{2}^{2}=\lambda^{2}\,Y^{\top}(\lambda I+H^{\top}H)^{-2}Y, which collapses the dependence on HH into a single Gram-like term H⊤​HH^{\top}H. We define the Gram-induced error function ℰλ​(Gσl)=Y⊤​(λ​I+Gσl)−2​Y\mathcal{E}_{\lambda}(G^{l}_{\sigma})=Y^{\top}(\lambda I+G^{l}_{\sigma})^{-2}Y, where Gσl=σ​(Wl​Hl)⊤​σ​(Wl​Hl)G^{l}_{\sigma}=\sigma(W_{l}H_{l})^{\top}\sigma(W_{l}H_{l}). We drop the superscript ll when the layer is clear from context.

However, 𝒯λ\mathcal{T}_{\lambda} still involves a squared matrix inverse and the nonlinearity σ\sigma inside GσG_{\sigma}, both of which obstruct direct analysis. To make the dependence on the Gram matrix tractable, we introduce a surrogate 𝒮⁡(G)=Y⊤​G​Y\mathcal{S}(G)=Y^{\top}GY. Here GG may denote either the nonlinear Gram Gσ=σ​(W​H)⊤​σ​(W​H)G_{\sigma}=\sigma(WH)^{\top}\sigma(WH) or the linearized Gram Gid=H⊤​W⊤​W​HG_{\mathrm{id}}=H^{\top}W^{\top}WH, in which the activation has been removed. The surrogate admits the following lower-bound relation to TL.

Theorem 2.

Let e0=‖Y−Y¯‖22e_{0}=\|Y-\bar{Y}\|_{2}^{2} and e1=‖Y‖2e_{1}=\|Y\|_{2}, and assume ‖W‖op≤c0\|W\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq c_{0}, ‖H‖F≤c1\|H\|_{F}\leq c_{1}, and N>dN>d. Then

𝒯λ​(H,Y)≥1−C⋅𝒮​(Gid)−1,\mathcal{T}_{\lambda}(H,Y)\geq 1-C\cdot\mathcal{S}(G_{\mathrm{id}})^{-1},

for some fixed constant CC.

Theorem 2 yields two benefits. First, the surrogate removes both the nonlinearity and the squared matrix inverse that obstruct direct analysis of 𝒯λ\mathcal{T}_{\lambda}. Second, 𝒮⁡(Gid)=Y⊤​H⊤​W⊤​W​H​Y\mathcal{S}(G_{\mathrm{id}})=Y^{\top}H^{\top}W^{\top}WHY exposes the weight Gram matrix W⊤​WW^{\top}W explicitly, connecting the analysis of TL to the results of Section 3. The proof is given in Section C.3. We now use this surrogate to study how how feature evolves during training and across layers.

4.2 Training & Layer-wise Dynamics

Training Dynamics

We now analyze how 𝒮⁡(Gid)\mathcal{S}(G_{\mathrm{id}}) evolves under GD. Throughout this subsection, we largely depend on a first-order Taylor expansion to characterize the leading-order behavior and see what this approach reveals about dominant portion of feature dynamics. We assume ff is mm-positively homogeneous in hh: f⁡(α​h)=αm​f​(h)f(\alpha h)=\alpha^{m}f(h) for any positive scalar α\alpha. We further assess the validity of this approach empirically in settings that go beyond these assumptions, including GELU activations in Section 4.3; further discussion and theoretical justification of our approach are in Section A.2.

Theorem 3.

For any loss function ℒ\mathcal{L}, let Gid=H⊤​W⊤​W​HG_{\mathrm{id}}=H^{\top}W^{\top}WH and Gid+=H⊤​(W+)⊤​W+​HG_{\mathrm{id}}^{+}=H^{\top}(W^{+})^{\top}W^{+}H, where W+=W−γ​∇WℒW^{+}=W-\gamma\nabla_{W}\mathcal{L}. If ff is 11-positively homogeneous in hh, the following holds:

𝒮⁡(Gid+)−𝒮⁡(Gid)≈2​γ​(f⊤​y)⋅(y⊤​K​g),\mathcal{S}(G_{\mathrm{id}}^{+})-\mathcal{S}(G_{\mathrm{id}})\approx 2\gamma\,(f^{\top}y)\cdot(y^{\top}Kg),

where Ki​j=hi⊤​hjK_{ij}=h_{i}^{\top}h_{j}, fi=f⁡(hi)f_{i}=f(h_{i}) are the predictions on the training set, and g=−∇fℒg=-\nabla_{f}\mathcal{L}.33 3 The same result extends to general mm-positively homogeneous case under the centered label assumption, ∑iyi=0\sum_{i}y_{i}=0.

Proof Sketch.

We rewrite (W+)⊤​W+−W⊤​W(W^{+})^{\top}W^{+}-W^{\top}W using the FL equation (Equation 1), decompose ∇hℒ=−∇hf⋅g\nabla_{h}\mathcal{L}=-\nabla_{h}f\cdot g, and resolve the cross terms hi⊤​∇hkfh_{i}^{\top}\nabla_{h_{k}}f via the mm-homogeneity identity hi⊤​∇hkf≈f⁡(hi)+(m−1)​f​(hk)h_{i}^{\top}\nabla_{h_{k}}f\approx f(h_{i})+(m-1)f(h_{k}) (Lemma 3). The full proof is in Section C.4. ∎

The term f⊤​yf^{\top}y captures the empirical correlation between predictions and labels. At initialization it is near zero, and as training proceeds it grows positive as ff aligns with yy.

To build intuition for y⊤​K​gy^{\top}Kg, consider the binary classification setting. Under the binary cross-entropy loss with sigmoid predictions, y^=sigmoid​(f⁡(x))∈(0,1)n\hat{y}=\text{sigmoid}(f(x))\in(0,1)^{n}, and labels y∈{0,1}ny\in\{0,1\}^{n}, the negative gradient takes the form g=y−y^g=y-\hat{y}, so gi>0g_{i}>0 when yi=1y_{i}=1 and gi<0g_{i}<0 when yi=0y_{i}=0. Writing the quantity in feature space yields

y⊤​K​g=(H​y)⊤​(H​g)=⟨∑i∈S1hi,∑j∈S1(1−y^j)​hj−∑k∈S0y^k​hk⟩,\displaystyle y^{\top}Kg=(Hy)^{\top}(Hg)=\langle\sum_{i\in S_{1}}h_{i},\;\sum_{j\in S_{1}}(1-\hat{y}_{j})\,h_{j}-\sum_{k\in S_{0}}\hat{y}_{k}\,h_{k}\rangle,

where Sa={i:yi=a}S_{a}=\{i:y_{i}=a\}. y⊤​K​gy^{\top}Kg measures the correlation, in feature space, between the positive-class centroid and a residual direction that pulls toward positive examples while pushing away from negative examples. Under feature learning regime where representations cluster by class, as ⟨hi,hj⟩≥⟨hi,hk⟩\langle h_{i},h_{j}\rangle\geq\langle h_{i},h_{k}\rangle holds for i,j∈S1,k∈S0i,j\in S_{1},k\in S_{0}. This makes the inner product positive whenever within-class similarity dominates cross-class similarity, before it tapers to zero as y^→y\hat{y}\rightarrow y.

A sharper interpretation of this gap comes from relating yy to a classical statistical object. Let fOLS=H⊤​(H​H⊤)−1​H​yf_{\mathrm{OLS}}=H^{\top}(HH^{\top})^{-1}Hy be the best linear predictor from current features. A direct calculation gives ‖y−fOLS‖K=0\|y-f_{\mathrm{OLS}}\|_{K}=0, so yy and fOLSf_{\mathrm{OLS}} coincide under the KK-norm. As training proceeds, ff moves toward yy and as a result f→fOLSf\rightarrow f_{\mathrm{OLS}} in KK-norm, while fOLSf_{\mathrm{OLS}} itself moves toward yy as TL increases.

This identifies feature learning as a moving-target problem. The network ftf_{t} chases fOLS,tf_{\mathrm{OLS},t}, but fOLS,t+1f_{\mathrm{OLS},t+1} itself is reshaped as features Ht+1H_{t+1} evolve: each gradient step closes the residual ‖fOLS,t−ft‖Kt\|f_{\mathrm{OLS},t}-f_{t}\|_{K_{t}} while simultaneously reopening it through feature updates that shift fOLS,t+1f_{\mathrm{OLS},t+1} toward yy. This contrasts sharply with the NTK regime [16], where, at infinite width, the kernel remains effectively fixed during training, and learning reduces to kernel regression in the corresponding RKHS [41]. In this regime, the solution is determined by the initial kernel, and training corresponds to fitting yy within this static function space, without additional parametrization such as μ​P\mu P [50]. The lazy regime corresponds to this linearized setting in which the feature map remains effectively fixed, whereas in the feature learning regime the evolving representation HtH_{t} induces a sequence of changing targets fOLS,tf_{\mathrm{OLS},t}, so that optimizing ftf_{t} simultaneously reshapes the feature geometry itself (Figure 3). We empirically compare these two regimes in Section B.4.

Layer-wise Dynamics

The role of depth in neural networks has been empirically validated in many practical architectures [14, 47], yet a unified theoretical account remains limited. Most existing work studies depth from an approximation perspective, showing that function composition is fundamentally more expressive than shallow expansion [44]. This line of work asks what functions are learnable with depth, rather than how a learned deep network processes input across its layers.

For the derivation we assume the Neural Feature Ansatz [39] holds. 6 discuss why the NFA usually holds and the degenerate cases under which it does not. Under the NFA, we show that an interpolating (i.e., sufficiently trained) network sequentially linearizes input data toward the target at the final linear readout.

Theorem 4.

Let fl:hl↦f⁡(x)f_{l}:h_{l}\mapsto f(x) denote the subnetwork mapping the ll-th hidden state to the final output, and assume the activation σ\sigma is mm-positively homogeneous. Assume the network interpolates the training data and ∃C0>0​ s.t. ​‖Wl​Hl‖F2≥C0,∀l\exists C_{0}>0\text{ s.t. }\|W_{l}H_{l}\|^{2}_{F}\geq C_{0},\forall l. Under the Neural Feature Ansatz Wl⊤​Wl≈ClN​∑i∇hl,ifl​∇hl,ifl⊤W_{l}^{\top}W_{l}\approx\tfrac{C_{l}}{N}\sum_{i}\nabla_{h_{l,i}}f_{l}\,\nabla_{h_{l,i}}f_{l}^{\top} for layer-dependent constants Cl>0C_{l}>0, the surrogate satisfies

𝒮⁡(Gidl)​{≳C0​‖Y‖22​Φl−1,if ​m>1​ and ​∑iyi=0,≳C0​‖Y‖24​Ψl−1,if ​m=1​ and ​fl​ is piecewise linear,\mathcal{S}(G^{l}_{\mathrm{id}})\begin{cases}\gtrsim C_{0}\|Y\|_{2}^{2}\,\Phi^{-1}_{l},&\text{if }m>1\text{ and }\sum_{i}y_{i}=0,\\ \gtrsim C_{0}\|Y\|_{2}^{4}\,\Psi^{-1}_{l},&\text{if }m=1\text{ and }f_{l}\text{ is piecewise linear,}\end{cases}

where Φl−1\Phi^{-1}_{l} and Ψl−1\Psi^{-1}_{l} are monotonically increasing in ll.

Proof Sketch.

Using the NFA, we decompose the surrogate into a sum of terms of the form hl,i⊤​∇hl,jfh_{l,i}^{\top}\nabla_{h_{l,j}}f. A first-order Taylor expansion and homogeneity then gives 𝒮⁡(Gidl)≈Cl​‖Y‖24\mathcal{S}(G^{l}_{\mathrm{id}})\approx C_{l}\|Y\|_{2}^{4} for both cases. Similarly, the NFA lets us decompose ‖Wl​Hl‖F2=tr⁡(Hl⊤​Wl⊤​Wl​Hl)≥C0\|W_{l}H_{l}\|_{F}^{2}=\mathrm{tr}(H_{l}^{\top}W_{l}^{\top}W_{l}H_{l})\geq C_{0}. Relating the two expressions shows that the lower bound of ClC_{l} is monotonically increasing in ll. The full proof is in Section C.5. ∎

The two cases of Theorem 4 differ in how the layer-wise complexity is measured. In the smooth mm-homogeneous case (m>1m>1), Φl\Phi_{l} is governed by the homogeneity gap ∝mL−l\propto m^{L-l}. In the piecewise-linear case (m=1m=1), the lower bound Ψl\Psi_{l} is governed by the number of linear regions of flf_{l} [33]. Both quantities measure the same thing from different angles: how far the subnetwork flf_{l} remains from being a linear function of its input. An interpolating network must produce yy from xx end-to-end, and Φl\Phi_{l} (or Ψl\Psi_{l}) measures the nonlinearity flf_{l} still has to supply to close the gap between hlh_{l} and yy. At shallow layers, flf_{l} does most of the work and the complexity is large; at deep layers, flf_{l} approaches a linear map and the complexity shrinks. Depth is the mechanism by which the total required nonlinearity is distributed across layers, and the surrogate 𝒮⁡(Gidl)\mathcal{S}(G^{l}_{\mathrm{id}}) — inversely proportional to Φl\Phi_{l} or Ψl\Psi_{l} — correspondingly grows with depth.

This formalizes sequential linearization: as ll increases, the residual nonlinearity flf_{l} must supply shrinks, and the network leaves a progressively more linear problem for subsequent layers. The picture matches the standard empirical observation underlying linear probes [2]: deeper layers admit higher-accuracy linear classifiers, because by the time data reaches them, much of the nonlinear work has already been done.

4.3 Empirical Validation

We train a four-layer fully connected network with hidden dimension 256 and GELU activations [15] on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 [22], using SGD with learning rate 0.0050.005 for 100 epochs. To extend the Target Linearity to the multiple target cases, we extend the surrogate to multi-class classification by replacing YY with the one-hot label matrix Y∈ℝN×CY\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times C} and redefining the surrogate as 𝒮cls​(G)=tr⁡(Y⊤​G​Y)\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{cls}}(G)=\mathrm{tr}(Y^{\top}GY). Since tr⁡(Y⊤​G​Y)=∑cyc⊤​G​yc\mathrm{tr}(Y^{\top}GY)=\sum_{c}y_{c}^{\top}Gy_{c}, the dynamics from Section 4.2 carry over directly.

Figure 4 reports the training and layer-wise dynamics of the surrogate 𝒮cls​(Gidl)\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{cls}}(G^{l}_{\mathrm{id}}) and TL (λ=0\lambda=0) at each layer. Both quantities grow throughout training, consistent with the regime identified in Theorem 3, and both increase with layer index, consistent with the sequential linearization predicted by Theorem 4. The surrogate grows roughly exponentially while TL grows roughly logarithmically; this is consistent with Theorem 2, where the lower bound on TL involves the inverse of the surrogate. Analogous results for the Adam optimizer [19] are in Section B.5.

A notable benefit of TL is that, by being defined as the R2R^{2} of regression onto the target, it applies to any task with a continuous target — not just classification. We confirm this on self-supervised generation: TL grows during VAE training [20] when the target is the reconstructed input (Section B.6). This positions TL as a unifying measure of feature learning across discriminative and generative tasks, in contrast to phenomena like Neural Collapse [36] that are formulated specifically for classification.

5 Link to Other Feature Learning Phenomena

The framework developed in Section 4 is general — TL is defined for any task with a target, and its dynamics are governed by the weight Gram matrix. We now show that this generality recovers two well-known feature learning phenomena as special cases of our framework: Neural Collapse [36] as the maximum case of our surrogate in classification, and the linear interpolation property of generative models [42] as a consequence of high TL in latent space.

Neural Collapse as an Extreme Case

In the classification setting, 36 report the Neural Collapse (NC) phenomenon, in which the penultimate-layer features of trained networks (NC1) collapse to their class means with vanishing within-class variation, and (NC2) form a simplex equiangular tight frame. Existing theoretical accounts of NC rely largely on the Unconstrained Feature Model [32], which treats hidden states as freely trainable variables; recent work has begun to relax this [31] but only under linear separability assumptions.

Proposition 2.

Consider f⁡(x)=W⊤​h​(x)+bf(x)=W^{\top}h(x)+b with hidden states centered (∑ih⁡(xi)=0\sum_{i}h(x_{i})=0), WW and bb trained under squared loss on the centered one-hot label matrix, and C≤DC\leq D. Under NC1 and NC2, 𝒮cls​(Gid)\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{cls}}(G_{\mathrm{id}}) attains the maximum value allowed by a norm constraint ‖Gid‖F≤c\|G_{\mathrm{id}}\|_{F}\leq c for some c>0c>0.

Proposition 2 positions NC corresponds to a maximally linearized representation in classification: the geometric structure observed empirically in trained networks [36] is precisely what saturates the surrogate 𝒮cls\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{cls}}. This recovers NC without invoking the Unconstrained Feature Model, instead deriving it from the same Gram-matrix framework that governs general feature learning. The full proof is in Section C.6. We note that 5 independently show that target linearity (in the form of kernel linearization) controls the rate of NC formation in deep Recursive Feature Machines.

Linear Interpolation Property in Generative Models

TL is defined as the R2R^{2} of regression, so it applies to any task with a continuous target. We use this to address a phenomenon in generative models: 42 observed that decoders of trained Variational Autoencoders [20] approximately respect linear interpolation in latent space, f⁡(α​z1+(1−α)​z2)≈α​x1+(1−α)​x2f(\alpha z_{1}+(1-\alpha)z_{2})\approx\alpha x_{1}+(1-\alpha)x_{2}, where ff is the decoder, ziz_{i} are latent codes, and xix_{i} are the corresponding inputs. This raises a natural question: when does a nonlinear decoder admit such linear interpolation?

Proposition 3.

Let Z=[z1,…,zN]⊤Z=[z_{1},\ldots,z_{N}]^{\top} be latent vectors and X=[x1,…,xN]⊤X=[x_{1},\ldots,x_{N}]^{\top} the corresponding inputs. Let g⁡(z)=z⊤​(Z⊤​Z)−1​Z⊤​Xg(z)=z^{\top}(Z^{\top}Z)^{-1}Z^{\top}X be the ordinary least-squares estimator, and assume g∈ℱg\in\mathcal{F}. Then for any α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1],

minf∈ℱ⁡1N2​∑i,j‖f⁡(α​zi+(1−α)​zj)−(α​xi+(1−α)​xj)‖2≤1N​∑i‖g⁡(zi)−xi‖2.\min_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\tfrac{1}{N^{2}}\sum_{i,j}\|f(\alpha z_{i}+(1-\alpha)z_{j})-(\alpha x_{i}+(1-\alpha)x_{j})\|_{2}\;\leq\;\tfrac{1}{N}\sum_{i}\|g(z_{i})-x_{i}\|_{2}.

The right-hand side is exactly the OLS reconstruction error, which equals square root of 1−𝒯0​(Z,X)1-\mathcal{T}_{0}(Z,X) up to normalization. Proposition 3 therefore states that whenever the function class contains the OLS predictor and the latent code admits high TL with respect to the inputs, the decoder can interpolate linearly. Figure 5 empirically validates this finding in MNIST trained VAE (from class 2 to 8) and the full proof is in Section C.7.

6 Related Work & Discussion

Related Work

Feature linearization has been observed empirically across several settings: [7] reported decreasing curvature of hidden representations with depth, and [2] showed linear probes attain higher accuracy at deeper layers. These observations are diagnostic; TL formalizes them as a quantity tied to the weight Gram matrix and explains, via the dynamics of Section 4.2, why such linearization emerges from training rather than treating it as a post-hoc finding.

More broadly, theoretical accounts of feature learning mainly fall into three streams: (1) case studies on structured targets [1, 3, 10, 11], whereas our results apply to general neural networks; (2) metric studies that propose descriptive measures of representation quality [8, 9, 21], which capture whether feature learning occurred but not how and why; and (3) phenomenon-driven studies that explain specific behaviors such as Neural Collapse [32, 36] or grokking [38, 27] in isolation. We aim to unify these threads by deriving feature dynamics directly from the Gram structure.

Closest to our analysis is the Neural Feature Ansatz [39], which conjectures Wl⊤​Wl∝𝔼⁡[∇hlf⋅∇hlf⊤]W_{l}^{\top}W_{l}\propto\mathbb{E}[\nabla_{h_{l}}f\cdot\nabla_{h_{l}}f^{\top}]. Our VCS captures the Gram update dynamics directly (Theorem 1) without invoking the ansatz, tracking the actual update at ρ=0.98\rho=0.98 versus 0.710.71 for AGOP. A more comprehensive literature review is in Section A.1.

Target Linearity in Pre-trained Transformer

We measure TL across every layer of BERT [12] on four downstream tasks comparing randomly initialized, pre-trained, and fine-tuned models in Section B.7. The goal is to check whether the dynamics theorized in Section 4.2 holds for complex transformers and track what TL illuminates on the pre-training and fine-tuning regime. We observe pre-training alone produces representations that are substantially more target linear with downstream labels than random initialization. Fine-tuning then converts this structure into a near-monotone TL profile that saturates within a single epoch and barely improves thereafter.

Link to Generalization

From Figure 4, TL exhibits an interesting pattern when compared to generalization performance. In both CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, the training accuracy exceeds 0.9, while the test accuracy differs significantly (50% in CIFAR-10 and 20% in CIFAR-100). Meanwhile, the TL values differ substantially: the last-layer TL exceeds 0.5 for CIFAR-10 but only 0.15 for CIFAR-100. This is particularly interesting because TL is measured on the training set, where both models achieve high accuracy. To further investigate this phenomenon, we evaluate TL on a random-label dataset [51] and a modular arithmetic dataset which exhibit grokking [38] in Section B.8.

Appendix A Related Works & Limitations

A.1 Comprehensive Related Works

As feature learning is one of the distinguishing advantages of neural networks over classical machine learning models (such as kernel machines), an emerging body of work has focused on characterizing both theoretical and empirical aspects of feature learning. From the theoretical side, the study of feature learning in neural networks has largely been focused on fully connected networks used for multi-index modeling [1, 3, 10, 11]. Specifically, multi-index models are functions f∗:ℝd→ℝf^{*}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} of the form f∗​(x)=g⁡(UT​x)f^{*}(x)=g(U^{T}x) where U∈ℝd×rU\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r} satisfies r<<dr<<d. It is known in such settings that neural networks outperform kernel machines by estimating the subspace UU through feature learning (see e.g., [10] for an example of such an argument). Select work [18] has also theoretically analyzed feature learning in more general neural network architectures such as convolutional networks. Additional work has studied feature learning in deep fully connected networks, identifying problem settings for which feature learning in 2-hidden layer networks leads to improved sample complexity over feature learning in 1-hidden layer networks [35].

As a step toward more broadly characterizing the mechanism of feature learning in neural networks, the work of [39] posited the Neural Feature Ansatz (NFA) stating that Gram matrices of weights in layer ℓ\ell of a neural network are proportional to the Average Gradient Outer Product (AGOP) of the network (where gradients are computed with respect into layer ℓ\ell). This work presented empirical evidence for this claim across fully connected networks, convolutional networks, recurrent networks and transformers. Follow up work [40] proved that the claim of [39] was true in deep linear networks used for low rank matrix completion (a prominent setting for studying feature learning [13]). Additional follow up work [6] showed that the NFA did not hold with exact proportionality for all data generating processes and instead connected Gram matrices with an alternative object (based on gradient of the loss and activations). Related theoretical work [37] also connected the Expected Gradient Outer Product (EGOP) with the implicit bias of fully connected networks with a single nonlinearity. In particular, this work showed that the representation cost of such networks was bounded by Schatten-norms of the EGOP (implying that networks with minimum representation cost also had low rank EGOPs).

Lastly, linearization of features is a prominent observation in neural networks that has been studied in several settings [2, 7, 30]. Recently, there has been renewed interest in understanding the linearization of features in transformer-based language models, where linear representations of concepts can be used to monitor and steer such models [4, 52].

A.2 Limitations

On First-Order Approximations

Our analysis of Target Linearity dynamics relies on first-order Taylor expansions, especially the homogeneity-based decompositions (Lemma 3). This is a deliberate trade-off. Existing dynamics analyses [1, 3, 10] achieve precise descriptions at the cost of restrictive assumptions on architecture or data. We aim for the opposite end of this trade-off: macroscopic dynamics under minimal technical assumptions, capturing leading-order behavior rather than exact trajectories.

While first-order approximations can be loose for individual terms given the highly nonlinear nature of deep networks, we conjecture that the aggregate quantities we study — particularly the surrogate 𝒮⁡(Gid)\mathcal{S}(G_{\mathrm{id}}), which sums over all training samples — are more robust than any individual term within them, in line with the concentration patterns observed in mean-field analyses [29, 43]. We view this approximation-based approach as complementary to exact analyses: trading precision for generality may surface phenomena, such as the sequential linearization of Section 4.2, that restricted exact analyses would not naturally reveal. The following proposition partially justifies this approach.

Proposition 4.

If a function ff is mm-positively homogeneous and input data and function values are centered, i.e., x¯=1N​∑ixi=0\bar{x}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}x_{i}=0 and ∑if⁡(xi)=0\sum_{i}f(x_{i})=0, then sum of all pairs of first-order Taylor approximation errors among each data points is zero.

Proof.

By writing the sum of first-order Taylor approximation errors,

∑i​j[f⁡(xi)−f⁡(xj)−(xi−xj)⊤​∇xjf]\displaystyle\sum_{ij}\left[f(x_{i})-f(x_{j})-(x_{i}-x_{j})^{\top}\nabla_{x_{j}}f\right] =∑i​jf⁡(xi)−∑i​jf⁡(xj)−∑i​j(xi−xj)⊤​∇xjf\displaystyle=\sum_{ij}f(x_{i})-\sum_{ij}f(x_{j})-\sum_{ij}(x_{i}-x_{j})^{\top}\nabla_{x_{j}}f
=−∑i​j(xi−xj)⊤∇xjf\displaystyle=-\sum_{ij}(x_{i}-x_{j})^{\top}\nabla_{x_{j}}f
=−N​x¯⊤​(∑j∇xjf)+N​∑jxj⊤​∇xjf\displaystyle=-N\bar{x}^{\top}\left(\sum_{j}\nabla_{x_{j}}f\right)+N\sum_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\nabla_{x_{j}}f
=N​∑jxj⊤​∇xjfas ​x¯=∑ixi=0\displaystyle=N\sum_{j}x_{j}^{\top}\nabla_{x_{j}}f\quad\text{as }\bar{x}=\sum_{i}x_{i}=0
=mN∑jf(xj)as f is homogeneous\displaystyle=mN\sum_{j}f(x_{j})\quad\text{as }f\text{ is homogeneous}
=0as ​∑if⁡(xi)=0\displaystyle=0\quad\text{as }\sum_{i}f(x_{i})=0

∎

On Technical Assumptions

Our analysis mainly adopts three assumptions that are standard in the deep learning theory literature: (i) m-positive homogeneity [17, 24, 28], satisfied exactly by bias-free ReLU networks; and (ii) lower-bounded pre-activation norm, which is automatically satisfied unless W​H=0WH=0 (a degenerate collapse). Additionally, the recent Neural Feature Ansatz [39] is adopted in dynamic analysis. NFA has been established theoretically in low-rank matrix completion, a widely studied setting for feature learning [40], and has also been validated empirically across a broad range of architectures and datasets. Additionally, 6 discuss why the NFA usually holds and the degenerate cases under which it does not. Although its theoretical foundations are not yet fully understood, our analysis relies on extensive empirical validation in the original work.

Appendix B Experiment Details & Additional Experiments

We use a machine with AMD Ryzen 9 5900X 12-Core Processor CPU with one NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU. Each experiment takes less than an hour, and the time can vary depending on the worker’s settings. We attach our code for full reproduction.

B.1 Gradient Whitening Experiment

We solve the following optimization problem:

argW+⁡min⁡‖W+−W‖Fsubject to(W+)⊤​W+=(W−γ​G)⊤​(W−γ​G),\arg_{W^{+}}\min\|W^{+}-W\|_{F}\quad\text{subject to}\quad(W^{+})^{\top}W^{+}=(W-\gamma G)^{\top}(W-\gamma G),

where G=∇WℒG=\nabla_{W}\mathcal{L}. By writing W+=W−γ​ΔW^{+}=W-\gamma\Delta, we can obtain the following problem:

argΔ⁡min⁡‖Δ‖F\displaystyle\arg_{\Delta}\min\|\Delta\|_{F}\quad subject to(W−γ​Δ)⊤​(W−γ​Δ)=(W−γ​G)⊤​(W−γ​G)\displaystyle\text{subject to}\quad(W-\gamma\Delta)^{\top}(W-\gamma\Delta)=(W-\gamma G)^{\top}(W-\gamma G)
⇔Δ⊤​W+W⊤​Δ≈G⊤​W+W⊤​G\displaystyle\Leftrightarrow\Delta^{\top}W+W^{\top}\Delta\approx G^{\top}W+W^{\top}G

which is approximately equivalent to the original problem:

argΔ′⁡min⁡‖G−Δ′‖F\displaystyle\arg_{\Delta^{\prime}}\min\|G-\Delta^{\prime}\|_{F}\quad subject toΔ′⁣⊤​W+W⊤​Δ′≈0\displaystyle\text{subject to}\quad\Delta^{\prime\top}W+W^{\top}\Delta^{\prime}\approx 0
⇔(W−γ​Δ′)⊤​(W−γ​Δ′)≈W⊤​W,\displaystyle\Leftrightarrow(W-\gamma\Delta^{\prime})^{\top}(W-\gamma\Delta^{\prime})\approx W^{\top}W,

by letting Δ=G−Δ′\Delta=G-\Delta^{\prime}.

Solution for the problem is well-known as an orthogonal procrustes problem:

W+=U​V⊤​W+~,W^{+}=UV^{\top}\tilde{W^{+}},

for singular value decomposition W​(W+~)⊤=U​Σ​V⊤W(\tilde{W^{+}})^{\top}=U\Sigma V^{\top} and any W+~\tilde{W^{+}} satisfying (W+)⊤​W+=(W−γ​G)⊤​(W−γ​G)(W^{+})^{\top}W^{+}=(W-\gamma G)^{\top}(W-\gamma G). By simply setting W+~=W−γ​G\tilde{W^{+}}=W-\gamma G, we apply the Newton-Schulz method similar to Muon optimizer [26] to compute U​V⊤UV^{\top}.

B.2 Gradient Whitening on Convolutional Neural Network

We present the gradient whitening results for a Convolutional Neural Network [23]. We train a model with 3 convolutional layers with 16 channels and 2-by-2 kernels, 2 max pooling layers, followed by a final linear classifier. We train the model using the SGD optimizer with a learning rate of 0.01 and momentum factor of 0.95 for 20 epochs. The result in Figure 6 shows negligible difference between original SGD and Gram-whitened SGD, similar to fully connected neural network case.

B.3 Virtual Covariance vs. AGOP

In this section, we compare weight Gram (W⊤​WW^{\top}W) with AGOP (1N​∑i=1N∇hif⋅∇hif⊤\tfrac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\nabla_{h_{i}}f\,\cdot\nabla_{h_{i}}f^{\top}) and the sum of our proposed VCS (∑t=1τcov~​(hl,t+)−cov~​(hl,t)\sum_{t=1}^{\tau}\widetilde{\mathrm{cov}}(h^{+}_{l,t})-\widetilde{\mathrm{cov}}(h_{l,t})). We employ a two-layer neural network with a hidden dimension of 256 and train it on the CIFAR-10 dataset [22] using SGD with a learning rate of 0.05. We use the GELU function [15] as a σ\sigma. The model achieves 46% accuracy on the evaluation dataset. We then plot the reshaped diagonal components of W⊤​WW^{\top}W, AGOP, and the sum of the VCS in Figure 7. We also compute the Pearson correlation ρ\rho between them.

We observe that both VC and AGOP exhibit a high correlation with the weight Gram. However, VC achieves a correlation of ρ≈0.98\rho\approx 0.98, which is substantially higher than that of AGOP (ρ≈0.71\rho\approx 0.71). This tendency is also evident in the visualizations: while both methods highlight the centered region, AGOP produces a relatively vague pattern, whereas VC closely resembles the weight Gram. Through this, we empirically verify that Theorem 1 holds, and the γ2\gamma^{2} factor does not significantly affect the resulting weight Gram.

B.4 Comparing Lazy vs. Rich Regims

We train standard-parameterization MLPs (depth 3, ReLU, no bias) of widths {32,128,512,1024}\{32,128,512,1024\} on a synthetic staircase target y=x1​x2​x3​x4+x1​x2​x3+x1​x2+x1y=x_{1}x_{2}x_{3}x_{4}+x_{1}x_{2}x_{3}+x_{1}x_{2}+x_{1} [1] with n=1000n=1000 Gaussian inputs in ℝ10\mathbb{R}^{10}. NTK Initialization [16] (std=1/fan​-​in\mathrm{std}=1/\sqrt{\mathrm{fan\text{-}in}}) and learning rate (0.010.01, full-batch SGD, 20002000 epochs) are held fixed across widths, so width alone interpolates between rich and lazy regimes. Every 2020 epochs we extract the penultimate features HH and record ‖y−yOLS‖2\|y-y_{\mathrm{OLS}}\|_{2}, ‖y^−yOLS‖2\|\hat{y}-y_{\mathrm{OLS}}\|_{2}, and ‖y−y^‖2\|y-\hat{y}\|_{2}, where yOLS=H⊤​(H​H⊤+ϵ​I)−1​H​yy_{\mathrm{OLS}}=H^{\top}(HH^{\top}+\epsilon I)^{-1}Hy.

By the triangle inequality, the training loss decomposes as ‖y^−y‖2≤‖y^−yOLS‖2+‖yOLS−y‖2\|\hat{y}-y\|_{2}\leq\|\hat{y}-y_{\mathrm{OLS}}\|_{2}+\|y_{\mathrm{OLS}}-y\|_{2}, isolating two distinct sources of progress: how well the network fits the best linear predictor in its current feature space, and how well that feature space can linearly express yy. Figure 8 shows that in the rich regime (widths 32,12832,128), both terms decrease substantially: y^\hat{y} chases yOLSy_{\mathrm{OLS}} while yOLSy_{\mathrm{OLS}} itself shifts toward yy as features reorganize. As width grows, this gap flattens; at width 10241024, ‖y−yOLS‖2\|y-y_{\mathrm{OLS}}\|_{2} stays near zero throughout training while ‖y^−yOLS‖2\|\hat{y}-y_{\mathrm{OLS}}\|_{2} alone drives the decrease in ‖y−y^‖2\|y-\hat{y}\|_{2}, recovering the lazy / NTK behavior in which learning reduces to kernel regression in a fixed feature space. Consequently, the rich regime achieves a lower final ‖y^−y‖2\|\hat{y}-y\|_{2} through successful feature learning, whereas the lazy regime is bottlenecked by the static expressivity of its initial features. This directly confirms the moving-target picture predicted in Section 4.2.

B.5 Target Linearity with ADAM Optimizer

We present the surrogate and TL values with ADAM [19] optimizer in Figure 9. Though our analysis mainly focused on the gradient descent optimizer, the results show a consistent pattern for various optimizers.

B.6 Target Linearity in Generative Model

We empirically measure how TL evolves in a self-supervised VAE [20] trained on an image generation task. Assuming Gaussianity of the latent vector, the (β\beta-)VAE is trained with the following loss function:

ℒ=−Eq⁡(z|x)​[log⁡p⁡(x|z)]⏟reconstruction error+βDK​L(q(z|x)||p(z))⏟regularization error,\mathcal{L}=\underbrace{-E_{q(z|x)}[\log p(x|z)]}_{\text{reconstruction error}}+\underbrace{\beta D_{KL}(q(z|x)||p(z))}_{\text{regularization error}},

where the regularization term controlled by β\beta constrains the latent space to follow a Gaussian distribution.

We train the VAE on two image datasets: MNIST and CIFAR-10. We use a 2-layer fully-connected neural network with hidden dimension 512 for both the encoder and decoder, and set the latent dimension to 32. The VAE is trained with the ADAM optimizer [19] with a learning rate of 0.0001 for 10 epochs for MNIST and 30 epochs for CIFAR-10. During training, we measure the TL between latent vectors ZZ and the prediction target XX. We visualize the TL along with the validation set reconstruction error for varying β\beta from 0.05 to 10.0. The results are shown in Figure 10.

The results demonstrate several key observations about the relationship between the regularization parameter β\beta, reconstruction quality, and TL in VAE training.

First, we observe a clear trade-off between reconstruction error and TL across different β\beta values. For both MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets, lower β\beta values (0.05, 0.1) achieve significantly lower reconstruction errors but also exhibit higher TL. Conversely, higher β\beta values (5.0, 10.0) result in increased reconstruction error while maintaining lower TL. This trade-off is visually evident in the generated images: lower β\beta values produce sharper, more detailed reconstructions that closely resemble the original images, whereas higher β\beta values yield increasingly blurred and abstract representations.

Second, the evolution of TL during training shows distinct patterns depending on β\beta. For low β\beta values (0.05, 0.1), TL steadily increases throughout training, suggesting that the latent representations become progressively more linearly related to the input as the model prioritizes reconstruction accuracy. In contrast, moderate to high β\beta values (1.0, 5.0, 10.0) maintain relatively stable or slightly increasing TL, indicating that stronger regularization constrains the latent space structure.

Finally, the generated samples reveal the practical implications of the β\beta parameter. For MNIST, even with β=10.0\beta=10.0, the digits remain somewhat recognizable, albeit heavily smoothed. However, for CIFAR-10, high β\beta values (β=10.0\beta=10.0) produce nearly uniform gray images with minimal structure, indicating that excessive regularization can completely collapse the model’s ability to capture meaningful image features in complex domains.

B.7 Target Linearity in Pre-trained Transformers

We fine-tune BERT [12] on four tasks spanning two task families: sequence classification (SST-2 and MNLI datasets [48]) and token classification (CoNLL-2003 POS tagging and NER datasets [46]). All models are trained for 3 epochs with AdamW [19] at learning rate 2e-5. To compute target linearity at each stage, we sample 2,000 training examples and reduce hidden states to 256 dimensions via PCA. We report TL for five model states per task: randomly initialized (architecture only), pre-trained (no fine-tuning), and the three fine-tuned epoch checkpoints. The results are in Figure 11.

Across all four tasks, the pre-trained model’s TL curve sits well above the randomly initialized baseline at every layer, despite the pre-training objective (MLM + NSP) never seeing any of these labels. This is the cleanest evidence in our experiments that pre-training does not merely produce a useful initialization for optimization but actually learns representations that are relatively linearly separable for downstream tasks. The size of the gap, however, depends sharply on how aligned the task is with the pre-training objective: it is largest for POS and NER (which depend on local lexical and syntactic regularities that MLM directly rewards), moderate for sentiment, and smallest for NLI — where the pre-trained TL barely separates from the random baseline. NLI requires cross-sentence reasoning that token-level reconstruction has little incentive to encode, so the linearly-extractable signal is correspondingly weaker.

Pre-training and fine-tuning produce qualitatively different layerwise profiles. The pre-trained curves recapitulate a pattern reported in earlier probing work [45]: TL for semantic tasks (sentiment) climbs monotonically toward the top of the network, while TL for syntactic tasks (POS, NER) peaks in the early-to-middle layers and slightly decays afterward. This is consistent with the view that BERT progressively assembles a classical NLP pipeline, with surface and syntactic information concentrated low and semantic information high. Fine-tuning, however, erases this division: after a single epoch, all four tasks exhibit the same near-monotone increasing TL profile, with the pre-trained curve serving as a lower envelope. Even POS — for which the pre-trained model’s optimal layer is layer 3 — is reorganized so that the final layer carries the most target linear information. This implies the layerwise specialization seen during pre-training appears to be a property of the pre-training objective rather than an intrinsic property of the architecture.

B.8 Target Linearity and Generalization

Random Label Memorization

From Figure 4, TL exhibits an interesting pattern when compared to generalization performance. In both CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, the training accuracy exceeds 0.9, while the test accuracy differs significantly. The model achieves over 50% test accuracy on CIFAR-10 but only over 20% on CIFAR-100, indicating a much larger generalization gap for CIFAR-100. The TL values also differ substantially: the last-layer TL exceeds 0.5 for CIFAR-10 but only 0.15 for CIFAR-100. This is particularly interesting because TL is measured on the training set, where both models achieve high accuracy. These results suggest a potential relationship between generalization and TL, although we do not provide a theoretical analysis.

To further investigate this phenomenon, we measure TL on randomly labeled datasets. It is well known that neural networks can memorize randomly labeled data, resulting in high generalization error [51]. We report TL values and train/test accuracy for various values of p∈[0,1]p\in[0,1], where pp denotes the fraction of data with randomly assigned labels. When p=0p=0, the labels are identical to the original dataset, whereas when p=1p=1, all labels are randomly shuffled. We train a 3-layer neural network with a hidden dimension of 256 on CIFAR-10 for 200 epochs to allow sufficient memorization. The model is optimized using stochastic gradient descent with a learning rate of 0.005. The results are presented in Figure 12.

Figure 12 shows that increasing the random label probability pp leads to both a larger generalization error and a decrease in last-layer TL. As pp increases, the overall training accuracy decreases up to p=0.5p=0.5, while it converges to approximately 0.70.7 for p≥0.75p\geq 0.75. In contrast, the test accuracy decreases more rapidly, from 0.50.5 (p=0.0p=0.0) to 0.30.3 (p=0.25p=0.25) and 0.20.2 (p=0.5p=0.5), resulting in an increasing generalization gap. Although the final training accuracy remains around 0.70.7 and the test accuracy around 0.10.1 for p≥0.75p\geq 0.75, higher values of pp require more training time to reach high training accuracy. As a result, during the middle stages of training, the generalization gap is larger for higher pp.

Interestingly, TL also decreases substantially: the last-layer TL drops from 0.450.45 (p=0.0p=0.0) to 0.30.3 (p=0.5p=0.5), while the training accuracy decreases from 0.850.85 to 0.750.75. TL in other layers also decreases over this range. For p≥0.75p\geq 0.75, the last-layer TL at the end of training remains around 0.250.25. However, similar to the slower increase in training accuracy, the growth of TL also slows for higher pp. Overall, the alignment between decreasing TL and an increasing generalization gap provides further evidence that TL may serve as a measure of generalization.

More interestingly, the TL of the middle layers exhibits a sudden increase for p≥0.75p\geq 0.75, unlike the cases with p≤0.75p\leq 0.75. This may indicate the need for additional layers to fully memorize highly randomized labels. For p≤0.75p\leq 0.75, the model can achieve sufficiently low loss using modestly processed intermediate representations exploiting the last layer, resulting in rapid early increases. However, for p≥0.75p\geq 0.75, the model explores the parameter space more extensively, showing slow early increases followed by sudden changes across multiple layers. This observation suggests that layer-wise TL patterns may reveal characteristics related to data complexity.

Grokking

Another interesting generalization-related phenomenon is grokking [38]. Grokking refers to a phenomenon in which a neural network first memorizes the training data with poor generalization, and only after prolonged training suddenly transitions to a solution that generalizes well. This behavior was observed in algorithmic tasks such as modular arithmetic, where models trained with standard optimization initially achieve near-perfect training accuracy while test accuracy remains low, followed by an abrupt improvement in generalization after many additional training steps. The transition is often associated with implicit regularization effects of optimization, such as weight decay, which gradually favor simpler or more structured solutions over memorizing ones.

Here, we examine how TL evolves under various grokking settings. We primarily vary the weight decay parameter λ\lambda, which is known to control the timing of grokking. We use a modular addition dataset with a prime modulus of 61. A 3-layer neural network with a hidden dimension of 256 is trained using the Adam optimizer [19] with a learning rate of 0.001 for 500 epochs. By varying λ∈(0,1)\lambda\in(0,1), we analyze how TL changes as grokking emerges. The results are presented in Figure 13.

Figure 13 shows diverse patterns of overfitting and grokking across different values of the weight decay parameter λ\lambda. One notable observation is that, for λ≥0.25\lambda\geq 0.25, TL continues to increase even after memorization, i.e., when the training accuracy is approximately 1.01.0. TL increases until grokking emerges and then saturates in the final stage of training. These results suggest a potential relationship between TL dynamics and generalization.

An interesting observation is that, as grokking emerges, the TL of the second layer (Layer 2) increases sharply. As a result, the gap between the second and last layers (Layer 3) narrows, although it widens again after generalization in the λ=0.75\lambda=0.75 case. For a more direct comparison, we plot the TL gap between the second and last layers alongside the generalization error in Figure 14. Although the TL gap increases after generalization, particularly for λ=0.75\lambda=0.75, it exhibits a similar decreasing pattern at the onset of grokking. These results suggest another potential use of layer-wise TL patterns as a measure of generalization.

Lemma 3.

C.5 Proof for Theorem 4

Statement 4.

Let fl:hl↦f⁡(x)f_{l}:h_{l}\mapsto f(x) denote the subnetwork mapping the ll-th hidden state to the final output, and assume the activation σ\sigma is mm-positively homogeneous. Assume the network interpolates the training data (f⁡(xi)≈yif(x_{i})\approx y_{i}, equivalently fl​(hl,i)≈yif_{l}(h_{l,i})\approx y_{i} for all ii and ll) and ∃C0>0​ s.t. ​‖Wl​Hl‖F2≥C0,∀l\exists C_{0}>0\text{ s.t. }\|W_{l}H_{l}\|^{2}_{F}\geq C_{0},\forall l. Under the Neural Feature Ansatz Wl⊤​Wl≈ClN​∑i∇hl,ifl​∇hl,ifl⊤W_{l}^{\top}W_{l}\approx\tfrac{C_{l}}{N}\sum_{i}\nabla_{h_{l,i}}f_{l}\,\nabla_{h_{l,i}}f_{l}^{\top} for layer-dependent constants Cl>0C_{l}>0, the surrogate satisfies

𝒮⁡(Gidl)​{≳C0​‖Y‖22​Φl−1,if ​m>1​ and ​∑iyi=0,≳C0​‖Y‖24​Ψl−1,if ​m=1​ and ​fl​ is piecewise linear,\mathcal{S}(G^{l}_{\mathrm{id}})\begin{cases}\gtrsim C_{0}\|Y\|_{2}^{2}\,\Phi^{-1}_{l},&\text{if }m>1\text{ and }\sum_{i}y_{i}=0,\\ \gtrsim C_{0}\|Y\|_{2}^{4}\,\Psi^{-1}_{l},&\text{if }m=1\text{ and }f_{l}\text{ is piecewise linear,}\end{cases}

where Φl−1\Phi^{-1}_{l} and Ψl−1\Psi^{-1}_{l} are monotonically increasing in ll.

For the first case (m>1m>1), we use Lemma 3, while for piecewise linear case, we use the following lemma.

Lemma 4.

For a ReLU network ff with bounded inputs ‖a‖2,‖b‖2<B\|a\|_{2},\|b\|_{2}<B, suppose that the gradient difference across any pair of adjacent linear regions is bounded by δ\delta, i.e.,

‖∇f​(x)−∇f​(y)‖2<δ,\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|_{2}<\delta,

for any xx and yy lying in two adjacent linear regions. Let MM denote the number of linear-region boundaries crossed by the segment [a,b][a,b]. Then

b⊤∇f(a)=f(b)+ϵ,where|ϵ|<2MBδ.b^{\top}\nabla f(a)=f(b)+\epsilon,\quad\text{where}\quad|\epsilon|<2MB\delta.
Proof of Lemma 4.

Recall the ReLU network ff is a 1-positively homogeneous and piece-wise linear function. By the fundamental theorem of calculus, for a piecewise linear function ff and points a,ba,b,

f⁡(b)−f⁡(a)\displaystyle f(b)-f(a) =∫01∇f(γ(t))⊤(b−a)dt\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{1}\nabla f(\gamma(t))^{\top}(b-a)\,dt
=∑j=0M(tj+1−tj)⋅vj⊤​(b−a),\displaystyle=\sum_{j=0}^{M}(t_{j+1}-t_{j})\cdot v_{j}^{\top}(b-a),

where γ⁡(t)=a+t⁡(b−a)\gamma(t)=a+t(b-a), the segment [a,b][a,b] crosses MM boundaries between linear regions at parameter values 0=t0<t1<⋯<tM<tM+1=10=t_{0}<t_{1}<\cdots<t_{M}<t_{M+1}=1, and vj=∇f​(γ​(t))v_{j}=\nabla f(\gamma(t)) for t∈(tj,tj+1)t\in(t_{j},t_{j+1}) denotes the (constant) gradient on the jj-th sub-interval. In particular, v0=∇f​(a)v_{0}=\nabla f(a) and vM=∇f​(b)v_{M}=\nabla f(b).

Subtracting the leading term v0⊤(b−a)=∇f(a)⊤(b−a)v_{0}^{\top}(b-a)=\nabla f(a)^{\top}(b-a) from both sides yields the first-order Taylor expansion with explicit remainder:

f⁡(b)\displaystyle f(b) =f(a)+∇f(a)⊤(b−a)−ϵ,\displaystyle=f(a)+\nabla f(a)^{\top}(b-a)-\epsilon,
ϵ\displaystyle\epsilon =∑j=1M(tj+1−tj)​(vj−v0)⊤​(b−a).\displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{M}(t_{j+1}-t_{j})(v_{j}-v_{0})^{\top}(b-a).

By the δ\delta bound of ∇f\nabla f for two adjacent linear regions, we have

‖vj−v0‖2=‖∑k=1jvk−vk−1‖2≤j​δ.\|v_{j}-v_{0}\|_{2}=\|\sum_{k=1}^{j}v_{k}-v_{k-1}\|_{2}\leq j\delta.

As all input points are normalized, ‖b−a‖2<2​B\|b-a\|_{2}<2B,

|ϵ|\displaystyle|\epsilon| ≤‖b−a‖2⋅∑j=1M(tj+1−tj)​‖vj−v0‖2\displaystyle\leq\|b-a\|_{2}\cdot\sum_{j=1}^{M}(t_{j+1}-t_{j})\|v_{j}-v_{0}\|_{2}
≤2​B​δ​∑j=1M(tj+1−tj)​j\displaystyle\leq 2B\delta\sum_{j=1}^{M}(t_{j+1}-t_{j})j
=2​B​δ​∑j=1M(tj+1−tj)​∑k=1j1\displaystyle=2B\delta\sum_{j=1}^{M}(t_{j+1}-t_{j})\sum_{k=1}^{j}1
=2Bδ∑j=1M∑k=1M(tj+1−tj)𝟏{k≤j}\displaystyle=2B\delta\sum_{j=1}^{M}\sum_{k=1}^{M}(t_{j+1}-t_{j})\mathbf{1}_{\{k\leq j\}}
=2​B​δ​∑k=1M∑j=kM(tj+1−tj)\displaystyle=2B\delta\sum_{k=1}^{M}\sum_{j=k}^{M}(t_{j+1}-t_{j})
=2​B​δ​∑k=1M(1−tk)≤2​M​B​δ\displaystyle=2B\delta\sum_{k=1}^{M}(1-t_{k})\leq 2MB\delta

Since f(a)=a⊤∇f(a)f(a)=a^{\top}\nabla f(a) holds by the 11-homogeneity, the result holds. ∎

From Lemma 3, we showed that via Taylor expansion, b⊤∇f(a)b^{\top}\nabla f(a) can be approximated by f⁡(b)f(b) for 11-homogeneous ff. In Lemma 4, we characterize the approximation error, which is analogous to the norm of the Hessian. However, the Hessian does not exist for piecewise-linear functions, as the second-order derivative is zero within linear regions and undefined at the boundaries. We therefore measure a generalized notion of the Hessian in terms of the number of boundaries between linear regions, and use it to bound ϵ\epsilon. Lemma 4 intuitively shows the error of the first order Taylor expansion can be bounded by the function complexity measured by the number of jumps (MM) and the degree of the jump (δ\delta).

Now we prove the main theorem.

Proof.

As we focus on the fixed ll-th layer, we omit the ll superscripts. We can write 𝒮⁡(Gidl)=∑i​j𝒮​(Gidl)i​j\mathcal{S}(G^{l}_{\mathrm{id}})=\sum_{ij}\mathcal{S}(G^{l}_{\mathrm{id}})_{ij} where 𝒮​(Gidl)i​j=yi​yj​hi⊤​W⊤​W​hj\mathcal{S}(G^{l}_{\mathrm{id}})_{ij}=y_{i}y_{j}h_{i}^{\top}W^{\top}Wh_{j}. By applying the Neural Feature Ansatz,

C.6 Proof for Proposition 2

Statement 5.

Consider f⁡(x)=W⊤​h​(x)+bf(x)=W^{\top}h(x)+b with hidden states centered (∑ih⁡(xi)=0\sum_{i}h(x_{i})=0), WW and bb trained under squared loss on the centered one-hot label matrix, and C≤DC\leq D. The surrogate 𝒮cls​(Gid)\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{cls}}(G_{\mathrm{id}}) attains the maximum value allowed by a norm constraint ‖Gid‖F≤c\|G_{\mathrm{id}}\|_{F}\leq c for some c>0c>0 under NC1 and NC2.

To prove the proposition, we need the following lemma.

Lemma 5.

For a matrix A∈ℝm×nA\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} and a symmetric matrix G∈ℝm×mG\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m} with bounded norm ‖G‖F≤c\|G\|_{F}\leq c, tr⁡[A⊤​G​A]\mathrm{tr}\left[A^{\top}GA\right] achieves its maximum value when G=c‖A​A⊤‖F​A​A⊤G=\frac{c}{\|AA^{\top}\|_{F}}AA^{\top}.

Proof of Lemma 5.

Note that tr⁡[A⊤​G​A]=tr⁡[G​A​A⊤]=⟨G,A​A⊤⟩F≤‖G‖F⋅‖A​A⊤‖F≤c​‖A​A⊤‖F\mathrm{tr}\left[A^{\top}GA\right]=\mathrm{tr}\left[GAA^{\top}\right]=\langle G,AA^{\top}\rangle_{F}\leq\|G\|_{F}\cdot\|AA^{\top}\|_{F}\leq c\|AA^{\top}\|_{F}, where equality holds when G=c‖A​A⊤‖F​A​A⊤G=\frac{c}{\|AA^{\top}\|_{F}}AA^{\top}. ∎

Now we prove the proposition.

Proof.

Since the hidden states are normalized, we can write the total, between-class, and within-class variation matrices as ΣT=Averagei​hi⋅hi⊤\Sigma_{T}=\mathrm{Average}_{i}h_{i}\cdot h_{i}^{\top}, ΣW=Averagec,i​(hi,c−μc)⋅(hi,c−μc)⊤\Sigma_{W}=\mathrm{Average}_{c,i}(h_{i,c}-\mu_{c})\cdot(h_{i,c}-\mu_{c})^{\top}, and ΣB=Averagec​μc⋅μc⊤\Sigma_{B}=\mathrm{Average}_{c}\mu_{c}\cdot\mu_{c}^{\top}, where hi,ch_{i,c} is the ii-th hidden state belonging to the cc-th class, and μc=Averagei​hi,c\mu_{c}=\mathrm{Average}_{i}h_{i,c} is the class mean vector. Let M=[μc]c=1CM=\left[\mu_{c}\right]_{c=1}^{C} be the class mean matrix. Note that ΣT=ΣB+ΣW\Sigma_{T}=\Sigma_{B}+\Sigma_{W}, and (NC1) implies ΣW=0\Sigma_{W}=0, so ΣT=ΣB\Sigma_{T}=\Sigma_{B}.

Following Proposition 1 in 36, the weight matrix satisfies:

W=1C​M⊤​ΣT+=1C​M⊤​ΣB+=M⊤​(M​M⊤)+=M+,W=\frac{1}{C}M^{\top}\Sigma_{T}^{+}=\frac{1}{C}M^{\top}\Sigma_{B}^{+}=M^{\top}(MM^{\top})^{+}=M^{+},

where ++ denotes the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse. The first equality holds by 49, and the second equality holds by the (NC1) condition. The third equality holds by the definition of ΣB\Sigma_{B}, and the last equality holds by properties of the pseudoinverse.

Since the number of classes CC is smaller than the hidden dimension DD and the hidden states form the simplex ETF (NC2), M+​M=I−1C​𝟏⋅𝟏⊤M^{+}M=I-\frac{1}{C}\mathbf{1}\cdot\mathbf{1}^{\top}. This implies M+​hi,c=M+​μcM^{+}h_{i,c}=M^{+}\mu_{c} is a centered one-hot vector with 1−1C1-\frac{1}{C} in the cc-th element and −1C-\frac{1}{C} the others, so that M+​H=Y⊤M^{+}H=Y^{\top}. Thus, the Gram matrix is Gid=H⊤​W⊤​W​H=Y​Y⊤G_{\mathrm{id}}=H^{\top}W^{\top}WH=YY^{\top} and the surrogate is 𝒮cls​(Gid)=tr⁡[Y⊤​Y​Y⊤​Y]\mathcal{S}_{\text{cls}}(G_{\mathrm{id}})=\mathrm{tr}\left[Y^{\top}YY^{\top}Y\right]. Lemma 5 shows that 𝒮cls​(Gid)\mathcal{S}_{\text{cls}}(G_{\mathrm{id}}) is maximized when Gid=‖Y​Y⊤‖F‖Y​Y⊤‖F​Y​Y⊤=Y​Y⊤G_{\mathrm{id}}=\frac{\|YY^{\top}\|_{F}}{\|YY^{\top}\|_{F}}YY^{\top}=YY^{\top}, which is achieved by setting c=‖Y​Y⊤‖Fc=\|YY^{\top}\|_{F}. ∎

C.7 Proof for Proposition 3

Statement 6.

Let Z=[z1,…,zN]⊤Z=[z_{1},\ldots,z_{N}]^{\top} be latent vectors and X=[x1,…,xN]⊤X=[x_{1},\ldots,x_{N}]^{\top} the corresponding inputs. minf∈ℱ⁡1N2​∑i,j‖f⁡(α​zi+(1−α)​zj)−(α​xi+(1−α)​xj)‖2≤1N​∑i‖g⁡(zi)−xi‖2.\min_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\tfrac{1}{N^{2}}\sum_{i,j}\|f(\alpha z_{i}+(1-\alpha)z_{j})-(\alpha x_{i}+(1-\alpha)x_{j})\|_{2}\;\leq\;\tfrac{1}{N}\sum_{i}\|g(z_{i})-x_{i}\|_{2}.
Proof.

Using the Triangle inequality,

‖f⁡(α​zi+(1−α)​zj)−(α​xi+(1−α)​xj)‖2\displaystyle\|f(\alpha z_{i}+(1-\alpha)z_{j})-(\alpha x_{i}+(1-\alpha)x_{j})\|_{2}

≤‖f⁡(α​zi+(1−α)​zj)−g⁡(α​zi+(1−α)​zj)‖2+‖g⁡(α​zi+(1−α)​zj)−(α​xi+(1−α)​xj)‖2.\displaystyle\leq\|f(\alpha z_{i}+(1-\alpha)z_{j})-g(\alpha z_{i}+(1-\alpha)z_{j})\|_{2}+\|g(\alpha z_{i}+(1-\alpha)z_{j})-(\alpha x_{i}+(1-\alpha)x_{j})\|_{2}.

So we obtain,

minf∈ℱ∑i​j\displaystyle\min_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\sum_{ij} ‖f⁡(α​zi+(1−α)​zj)−(α​xi+(1−α)​xj)‖2\displaystyle\|f(\alpha z_{i}+(1-\alpha)z_{j})-(\alpha x_{i}+(1-\alpha)x_{j})\|_{2}
≤min⁡∑i​jf∈ℱ⁡‖f⁡(α​zi+(1−α)​zj)−g⁡(α​zi+(1−α)​zj)‖2\displaystyle\leq\min_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\sum_{ij}\|f(\alpha z_{i}+(1-\alpha)z_{j})-g(\alpha z_{i}+(1-\alpha)z_{j})\|_{2}
+∑i​j∥g(αzi+(1−α)zj)−(αxi+(1−α)xj)∥2\displaystyle\quad\quad\quad\quad+\sum_{ij}\|g(\alpha z_{i}+(1-\alpha)z_{j})-(\alpha x_{i}+(1-\alpha)x_{j})\|_{2}

We can show the first term is 0 as g∈ℱg\in\mathcal{F}. For the second term, as gg is a linear function, we can show

g⁡(α​zi+(1−α)​zj)=α​g​(zi)+(1−α)​g​(zj).g(\alpha z_{i}+(1-\alpha)z_{j})=\alpha g(z_{i})+(1-\alpha)g(z_{j}).

Then the error term becomes

∑i​j\displaystyle\sum_{ij} ‖α​g​(zi)+(1−α)​g​(zj)−(α​xi+(1−α)​xj)‖2\displaystyle\|\alpha g(z_{i})+(1-\alpha)g(z_{j})-(\alpha x_{i}+(1-\alpha)x_{j})\|_{2}
≤∑i​jα​‖g⁡(zi)−xi‖2+(1−α)​‖g⁡(zj)−xj‖2\displaystyle\leq\sum_{ij}\alpha\|g(z_{i})-x_{i}\|_{2}+(1-\alpha)\|g(z_{j})-x_{j}\|_{2}
=α∑i​j∥g(zi)−xi∥2+(1−α)∑i​j∥g(zj)−xj∥2]\displaystyle=\alpha\sum_{ij}\|g(z_{i})-x_{i}\|_{2}+(1-\alpha)\sum_{ij}\|g(z_{j})-x_{j}\|_{2}]
